If the knights of ren decided to turn against the first order as a third party, would it be in character, and a clever move, for Hux to disguise a thermal detonator as a holocron, and putting it on

message.content: Assuming you mean placing it as a relic, peace offering, or “stolen artifact” in front of Kylo Ren or the Knights of Ren, it can be both in-character and clever for Hux, but only if it is motivated by political self-preservation. Hux is not a Force mystic, so he would not naturally think in terms of holocrons as sacred objects. However, he is a ruthless opportunist who understands power, reputation, and control. If the Knights of Ren have become a third-party threat, Hux might see a disguised thermal detonator as a way to eliminate Kylo Ren, destabilize the Knights, or frame them for the First Order’s own security crisis. The key is that Hux would not do it out of personal spite or random trickery; he would do it because he sees it as a way to protect the First Order’s hierarchy, or his own position within it. It would be a clever move because it exploits a very specific weakness: people with access to holocrons may be more suspicious of hidden Force tricks than of a standard military explosive. A thermal detonator shaped or cased to resemble a holocron could be treated with reverence, examined carefully, or placed near valuable objects, which increases the chance that someone will open it, move it, or activate it. It is also clever because it creates dramatic irony: the First Order would be using its own military technology to fake the one thing it fears, the Force. If the Knights of Ren are greedy, suspicious, or desperate to prove their independence, they might accept the object too eagerly. That makes the deception narratively satisfying, because the target’s assumptions become the trap. The main in-character problem is that Hux usually operates through orders, propaganda, bureaucracy, and public authority, so a crude booby trap must be made to look like strategy rather than a cheap assassination attempt. Hux would be more convincing if he did not personally place the detonator himself, but instead had an underling, a stormtrooper officer, or a spy do it while he maintained plausible deniability. That fits his role as a political operator: he wants results, but he also wants to remain above the mess. If the detonator backfires, Hux would not want to be the person who insulted Kylo Ren with a fake relic. Instead, he would want the failure to appear as a misunderstanding, a Knight’s betrayal, or a lower officer’s mistake. That is very Hux: use the system to kill your enemy, then let the system absorb the blame. To make the scene work, the detonator should be tied directly to the Knights’ betrayal and to Hux’s fear that Kylo Ren is becoming uncontrollable. Hux should recognize that a third-party Knights of Ren are dangerous because they could expose First Order weaknesses, turn against Snoke or the new leadership, or make Kylo Ren seem like a liability. A holocron-shaped thermal detonator could be presented as evidence, a reward, a diplomatic token, or a “recovered artifact” meant to prove the First Order’s strength. The cleverness would come from Hux using the language of the Force against the Force: he is not fighting Kylo with the dark side, he is fighting him with the First Order’s cold, mechanical logic. If Kylo or the Knights are too eager to claim the object, they fall for it; if they are cautious enough to test it first, Hux’s plan becomes a dangerous failure that can expose his machinations.
